strengths: Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art single-step TTA performance on AudioCaps across all metrics (FAD 1.77, FD 15.40) with only 120M parameters, and very low RTF (0.013); the model even surpasses multi-step baselines despite using 1 NFE.
Practically valuable: the model is trainable on consumer-grade GPUs (4x RTX 3090, ~53 hours total), which is a meaningful departure from most TTA work and improves reproducibility potential.

Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-4) that isolate the contributions of the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum, the flow field mix-up ratio, and the integrated CFG scale, with quantitative evidence for each design choice.

The proposed curriculum (pre-training on instantaneous field, fine-tuning on mixed fields) is a sensible, well-motivated stabilization strategy, and the ablation shows training mean flows from scratch is far less efficient (5x GPU hours, worse multi-step results), supporting the central claim.
Integrated CFG into the training target removes the guidance cost at inference, a practical benefit for single-step generation, and the CFG ablation is included.
Clear presentation of the method: Mean Flow preliminaries, architecture, and both training and inference algorithms are described precisely enough to reimplement.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core method is a direct application of MeanFlow (Geng et al. 2025) to the audio domain. The CFG integration and the r=t mix-up strategy are both adopted from prior work; the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum is the main new element, and it is a relatively straightforward two-stage fine-tuning scheme.

No human perceptual evaluation or listening tests. All conclusions rest on objective metrics (FAD, FD, KL, IS, CLAP), which are known to be imperfect proxies for perceptual quality, especially for fast/few-step generators. No audio samples are available in the submission (Project and Code links are empty), weakening claims of 'faithful' generation.

The curriculum ablation is partially confounded: MeanAudio_PT is trained on ALL datasets while the final MeanAudio is fine-tuned only on AudioCaps (AC), and notably MeanAudio_PT achieves a higher multi-step CLAP score (0.327 vs 0.321) than the final curriculum model, which is not discussed and slightly undercuts the claim that the curriculum is uniformly superior.
Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (AudioCaps test set); no Clotho or other evaluation sets are reported, making generalization claims hard to verify.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness: RTF is stated as 0.013 in the abstract/intro but 0.016 in the contributions; Table 2's footnote mentions 'all four datasets' while only three datasets are described; the text cites 'Figure 2' when referring to Table 2; several typos ('Prams', 'to synthesis an audio sample'). These do not undermine the core results but reduce polish.

Comparison fairness concerns: baselines are evaluated with official checkpoints, but dataset/training-scale differences across baselines (e.g., 2454 hours here vs. others) are not controlled; the 100x speedup headline compares against GenAU which uses 200 steps, a somewhat favorable framing.

Reproducibility is promised ('will open-source') but no code, weights, or project page is available at review time, and no ablation seeds/variance are reported despite nontrivial training instability discussed by the authors.

strengths: The paper presents the first application of the MeanFlow objective (Geng et al. 2025) to text-to-audio generation, and demonstrates convincingly strong empirical results: state-of-the-art single-step generation on AudioCaps (FAD 1.77, FD 15.40, RTF 0.013) with only 120M parameters, outperforming substantially larger accelerated and multi-step baselines.

The proposed instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow field mix-up is a sensible stabilization strategy, and it is supported by a thorough ablation program (curriculum vs. from-scratch training, mix-up ratios 0/25/50/75%, CFG scales 1-4) that isolates each component's contribution with consistent, interpretable trends.

Training cost is modest and clearly documented (three days on four RTX 3090s, ~96h+116h GPU-hours), making the work reproducible and accessible relative to larger TTA systems; the datasets, hyperparameters, timestep distributions, and architectural details are reported in sufficient depth to permit replication.

Integrating CFG into the training target to avoid extra NFEs at inference is practically valuable, and the True-NFE caveat in Table 1 (footnote distinguishing integrated-CFG models) shows careful, honest baseline accounting.

The writing is generally clear, the methodology is well-motivated with a coherent narrative (why mean flows alone struggle in the audio latent space, and how the curriculum addresses it), and the multi-step results show the model degrades gracefully rather than specializing solely in one-step generation.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a direct adaptation of an existing method (MeanFlow, Geng et al. 2025) to a new domain; the novelty lies mainly in the curriculum and domain-specific engineering (ConvMLP, dual text encoders, flow mix-up ratio), which is competent but incremental. The curriculum itself is a relatively intuitive two-stage pre-train-then-fine-tune scheme.

All quantitative evaluation is on a single benchmark (AudioCaps test set) with automatic metrics (FAD/FD/KL/IS/CLAP). There is no human listening study, no evaluation on Clotho or MusicCaps, and no qualitative examples in the paper, so perceptual claims of 'faithful' generation rest entirely on objective metrics that are known to imperfectly correlate with audio quality.

Reproducibility is promised but not yet demonstrated: the 'Project' and 'Code' links in the submission are placeholders, and no checkpoint is available at review time. For a paper whose central claims are empirical (SOTA single-step performance), the inability to inspect code or samples weakens verification.

There are internal inconsistencies that suggest insufficient polish: the abstract reports RTF 0.013 while the introduction states 0.016 for the same configuration; the text refers to 'Figure 2' when discussing the ablation (apparently meaning Table 2); and the curriculum section references training on 'all four datasets' though only three are described.

Baselines are somewhat favorable to the proposal: several strong recent accelerated TTA systems (e.g., Presto, Stable-Audio-Small, FlashAudio) are discussed in related work but not compared in Table 1, and the multi-step comparison mixes models trained with different data scales and CFG settings without controlling for training data, making the 'SOTA' claim only partially apples-to-apples.

Key design choices are justified empirically rather than analytically; e.g., why audio latents specifically destabilize the pure MeanFlow objective, and the interpretation of curriculum effects, would benefit from deeper analysis (loss curves, field alignment diagnostics) beyond final metric comparisons.

strengths: Strong empirical results: MeanAudio achieves state-of-the-art single-step TTA performance on the AudioCaps test set across all reported metrics (FAD 1.77, FD 15.40, KL 1.31, IS 9.78, CLAP 0.292), and remains competitive in multi-step generation despite using only 120M parameters versus 500M+ for most baselines.

Practical and efficient training regime: the model is teacher-free (no distillation), trains in ~2 days on four consumer RTX 3090 GPUs, and achieves an RTF of 0.013 — a genuinely useful practical contribution for deployment.

The instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow field mix-up is well-motivated and supported by a thorough ablation program (Table 2 curriculum ablation, Table 3 mix-up ratio sweep, Table 4 CFG scale sweep), which convincingly shows that both components are necessary: mixed-flow training from scratch converges slowly and the ratio 0% setting is unstable.

Integrating CFG into the training target is cleanly executed and eliminates the usual 2x NFE overhead; the paper is transparent about 'true NFE' vs. nominal NFE in Table 1, which aids fair comparison.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: architecture details (N1=4, N2=8, hidden dim 448), hyperparameters, training schedule, data filtering procedure against test leakage, and CLAP checkpoint are all specified, and the authors commit to releasing code and weights.
The paper is clearly written; the MeanFlow preliminary section makes the method accessible, and the two-stage curriculum is well illustrated (Figure 3, Algorithms 1-2).
weaknesses: Evaluation relies exclusively on automatic metrics (FD, FAD, KL, IS, CLAP). No human listening tests are reported, and CLAP score is a known weak proxy for perceptual faithfulness — a significant gap for a paper whose central claim is 'fast and faithful' generation.

Novelty is moderate: the core objective is directly adopted from MeanFlow (Geng et al. 2025); the main novel element is the two-stage curriculum with r=t mix-up, which is essentially a schedule over the fraction of flow-matching vs. mean-flow loss and is conceptually close to existing practices.

Internal inconsistencies and possible typos undermine polish: the abstract reports RTF 0.013 while the introduction reports 0.016; Table 2's footnote refers to 'all four datasets' while only three are described; Algorithm 1 line 8 mixes ω and w, and with ω=0.3, κ=0.9 the coefficient (1−ω−κ) is negative, leaving the guided-velocity combination and the claimed effective guidance scale ω/(1−κ) under-explained.

The headline '100x speedup' conflates few-step sampling with model size: MeanAudio is 120M parameters while GenAU is 1250M, so much of the RTF gap is attributable to parameter count rather than the MeanFlow objective; a same-size control would strengthen the claim.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: baselines were trained by others on different data scales and configurations (evaluated via official checkpoints), and several recent accelerated systems (e.g., Presto, Stable-Audio-Small, FlashAudio) are discussed but not included in the main comparison table.

No variance reporting, seed sensitivity, or statistical significance tests; several headline gains (e.g., single-step FAD 1.77 vs. ConsistencyTTA 2.31) could be sensitive to evaluation randomness given only one caption per test clip is sampled.

The stated motivation for the curriculum (model's own derivative providing poor guidance early in training) is plausible but only indirectly supported; a more direct diagnostic of training dynamics would increase confidence in the mechanism.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: slow inference is a genuine bottleneck for text-to-audio (TTA) deployment, and the paper convincingly demonstrates a 1-NFE generator with strong objective metrics (FD 14.30, CLAP 0.290) and the best reported RTF (0.013) on AudioCaps.

The adaptation of Mean Flows (Geng et al., 2025) to the TTA domain is technically sound: the Mean Flow identity, JVP-based target computation, and integrated CFG-into-training (avoiding the 2x NFE cost of sampling-time CFG) are correctly derived and clearly presented (Eqs. 2-3, Algorithms 1-2).

The instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow-field mix-up is a sensible and well-validated contribution to training stability; the ablations (Tables 3-4) show it is decisive — the pure mean-flow objective fails to converge and the r=t mix ratio strongly affects both single- and multi-step quality.

Comprehensive empirical support: comparisons against 10+ diffusion/flow baselines and accelerated models, subjective evaluation with 10 audio professionals, and additional ablations over architecture (CLAP, RoPE, ConvMLP), CFG scale, dataset/model scaling, and MusicCaps text-to-music generation.

Reasonable compute footprint (120M params, ~70 GPU-hours total on 4x RTX 3090) makes the work accessible, and the authors commit to full codebase and weight release; implementation details (hyperparameters, dataset construction in Appendix D) are sufficiently detailed for reproduction.
Writing is clear, the architecture figure is informative, and limitations are honestly discussed (10s truncation, noisy weak labels, no speech).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core learning objective is directly adopted from Mean Flows; the dual-encoder (FLAN-T5 + CLAP) conditioning, MM-DiT/DiT hybrid, RoPE, RMSNorm, SiWGLU, and ConvMLP are all established components assembled from Flux/SD3-style designs. The main novel elements (integrated CFG for mean flows in audio, the two-stage curriculum with r=t mix-up) are incremental training refinements rather than new principles.

Some fairness concerns in the main comparison: MeanAudio is trained on ~2.8M pairs (7801h) assembled from multiple corpora with LLM/MLLM-generated captions, whereas several baselines (e.g., TangoFlux, AudioLCM) use substantially less or different training data; the headline SOTA claim would be stronger with a data-controlled comparison. The main-table configuration (S-Full vs. S-AC) is also not always transparent in Table 1.

Ablation studies are performed on a reduced setup (AudioCaps only, 200k steps from the FluxAudio initialization), so the conclusions about mix-up ratios and architectural components may not transfer to the final full-data configuration; the r=0 case failing to converge is suggestive but not deeply analyzed (no diagnostic of why the mean-flow objective is unstable in the audio latent space).

Subjective evaluation covers only 10 prompts per model with 10 raters, and no statistical significance analysis is reported; CLAP/FD/FAD metrics for audio generation are known to be noisy proxies, which makes the margins over TangoFlux (e.g., FD 14.30 vs. 14.58 at very different NFE) harder to interpret.

Small presentation issues: 'Prams' typo in Table 1 and Table 7, the 'hidden dimension of 20' for latents is confusingly phrased, Figure 1 conflates differently-trained systems, and the effective guidance scale construction (ω, κ with negative unconditional weight) deserves a cleaner justification.

The paper does not compare against concurrent one-step audio approaches trained with similar mean/average-velocity objectives (e.g., variants of consistency or shortcut models for audio), so the specific advantage of MeanFlow over alternative one-NFE formulations is not isolated.

strengths: Comprehensive and transparent experimental design: objective metrics (FD, FAD, KL, IS, CLAP, RTF) plus a human study with 10 audio experts, evaluated on standard AudioCaps test splits with re-evaluated open-source baselines using official checkpoints, which strengthens comparability.

The instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow-field mix-up (Tables 3-4) is a genuine, well-motivated technical contribution beyond directly porting MeanFlow to audio; the ablation clearly shows the mean-flow objective alone fails to converge and quantifies the effect of the r=t mixing ratio.

Impressive efficiency results: single-step generation with RTF 0.013 and strong FD/CLAP scores from a compact 120M-parameter model, with detailed training-cost reporting (48h + 22h on 4x RTX 3090) that supports claims of trainability on consumer hardware.

Thorough ablation coverage (training curriculum, mix-up ratio, architectural components, CFG scale), plus additional data/model scaling and text-to-music experiments in the appendix that probe generalization.

Clear promise of full codebase and model weight release, and the training/inference procedures are specified at a level of detail (hyperparameters, timestep sampling, guidance formulation) that should support reproduction once artifacts are available.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core objective is directly adopted from Mean Flows (Geng et al., 2025), and most architectural refinements (RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, ConvMLP, dual-encoder conditioning, AdaLN) are established components from Flux and prior TTA work; the contribution is primarily a domain application plus engineering and stabilization tricks, which may fall short of the main-conference novelty bar.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: the 'Code' and 'Demo' links in the paper appear empty, and the 2.8M-pair aggregate training set is assembled from multiple sources with LLM/MLLM-generated captions whose exact construction (and licensing/copyright status of AudioSet, FreeSound, BBC contents) is not fully specified.

Some claims of SOTA require qualification: single-step IS (10.02) remains well below multi-step baselines like TangoFlux (12.81), and comparisons across accelerated models involve different backbones, VAEs, vocoders, and training data, so metric gains cannot be attributed solely to the MeanFlow objective.

Ablation studies are trained from scratch on AudioCaps only for 200k steps, which may not faithfully reflect the behavior of the final model pre-trained on 2.8M pairs; conclusions from Table 3-6 may not transfer to the full configuration.

Human evaluation is small-scale (10 raters, 10 prompts per condition per rater) with no inter-rater reliability or significance analysis reported, and no confidence intervals on the objective metrics.

The instantaneous-to-mean curriculum is justified post-hoc (instability of direct mean-flow training in the audio latent space) without a theoretical analysis of why audio latents are harder than images, and only one fine-tuning dataset/schedule is explored for the curriculum.

strengths: Strong empirical results: MeanAudio achieves clear SOTA among single-step (1-NFE) TTA models on AudioCaps (FD 14.30, CLAP 0.290) with a very low RTF of 0.013, and remains competitive in multi-step generation with a compact 120M-parameter backbone — a meaningful practical advance over heavier diffusion/flow baselines.

The two training contributions — integrated CFG in the mean-flow objective (avoiding doubled NFE at sampling time) and the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow-field mix-up — are well-motivated, clearly formalized (Algorithms 1–2, Figure 3), and directly address the documented instability of applying MeanFlow to audio latents.

Comprehensive ablation studies (training curriculum, r=t mix-up ratio, dual encoders, RoPE, ConvMLP, CFG scale) plus data/model scaling and text-to-music transfer experiments (Appendix C) substantially strengthen the empirical claims and provide useful best practices for future MeanFlow-based audio generators.

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed implementation hyperparameters, dataset statistics (Table 10), training cost (48h pre-training + 22h fine-tuning on 4× RTX 3090), explicit metric definitions (PANNs-based FD/IS/KL, VGGish FAD, CLAP checkpoint), a subjective evaluation protocol with 10 raters, and a commitment to release code and weights.
Both objective metrics and human evaluation (OVL/REL) consistently support the claims, and the paper is honest about limitations (10s truncation, noisy weak labels, no speech generation).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core idea is a direct application of MeanFlow (Geng et al., 2025) to the TTA domain. The architectural refinements (RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, ConvMLP, dual encoders) and curriculum are sensible engineering but largely incremental; the 'first MeanFlow TTA generator' framing reflects domain transfer more than a new method.

Potential comparability issues in Table 1: MeanAudio is trained on ~2.8M audio-text pairs, while several baselines (e.g., TangoFlux, AudioLCM) were trained on much smaller or different datasets; the SOTA claim should be interpreted with this data advantage in mind, and the paper does not fully discuss this confound.

Dataset statistics contain apparent inconsistencies: the text claims 2.8M pairs / 8k hours, but Table 10 entries sum to roughly 3.8M clips; LP-MusicCaps-MC is listed as 2.3M clips with only 6.3h duration (impossible), while Appendix D elsewhere says LP-MusicCaps contains ~25k segments. These errors undermine confidence in the data pipeline description.
The 'Code:' and 'Demo:' footnotes are empty in the manuscript, so the promised artifacts cannot be verified at review time; the reproducibility claim currently rests on descriptions alone.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported for objective metrics (FAD, FD, KL, IS, CLAP), and ablations are trained on AudioCaps only (200k steps), so some conclusions about the full 2.8M-pair model rely on extrapolation.

Relevance to the core ACL audience is moderate: TTA is a valid speech/multimedia topic, but the paper's framing and evaluation are closer to the audio/speech community (Interspeech/ICASSP) than to NLP; the text-encoder design analysis is the main NLP-relevant thread.
